title: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary of equal-length words, find the length of the shortest transformation sequence that changes one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in the dictionary. Explain the breadth-first search solution, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Word Ladder (Shortest Transformation Chain One Letter at a Time)

s1_definition.profdef: Word Ladder is a shortest path problem on an implicit graph where each word is a node and an edge connects two words that differ by exactly one letter. Because every edge has the same unit cost, breadth-first search from the begin word finds the fewest transformations to reach the end word. We generate neighbours on the fly by trying every single-letter change and keeping only those present in the dictionary.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India migrates an old product code to a new one, but compliance forces every intermediate code to be a valid registered code in the catalogue, changing one character at a time. We want the shortest valid chain of codes from the old to the new.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each word is a node, one-letter changes are edges, so BFS gives the shortest valid chain.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Ladder is a shortest path problem on an implicit graph where each word is a node and an edge connects two words that differ by exactly one letter. Because every edge has the same unit cost, breadth-first search from the begin word finds the fewest transformations to reach the end word. We generate neighbours on the fly by trying every single-letter change and keeping only those present in the dictionary.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India migrates an old product code to a new one, but compliance forces every intermediate code to be a valid registered code in the catalogue, changing one character at a time. We want the shortest valid chain of codes from the old to the new.

**One line to remember:** Each word is a node, one-letter changes are edges, so BFS gives the shortest valid chain.

sections.s2_technical:
We put all dictionary words into a hash set for constant-time membership checks, then run breadth-first search starting from the begin word at distance one. For the word at the front of the queue we generate every neighbour by replacing each position with each letter from a to z, and if the generated word is in the set we add it to the queue with distance plus one and remove it from the set so we never revisit it. The first time we generate the end word, its distance is the shortest chain length. Removing visited words from the set is how we mark them visited without a separate structure.

The neighbour generation is `for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) { char old = arr[i]; for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'z'; c++) { arr[i] = c; String next = new String(arr); if (dict.remove(next)) queue.add(next); } arr[i] = old; }`. A concrete check: from HIT to COG with dictionary HOT, DOT, DOG, LOT, LOG, COG, BFS finds HIT, HOT, DOT, DOG, COG, a length of five. Senior nuance: the complexity is order of N times L times 26 where N is the dictionary size and L is the word length, and a bidirectional BFS from both ends can dramatically cut the explored frontier.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is retiring an old product code and must transform it into a new product code, but a compliance rule says every intermediate code must already exist in the official catalogue and only one character may change at each step. We want the shortest valid sequence of code changes so the migration touches as few intermediate codes as possible. This is exactly how Word Ladder works: it finds the fewest one-character steps through a dictionary of valid codes.

The code defines a `ProductCodeMigrationService` with `shortestChain(begin, end, dictionary)` that runs breadth-first search. A `Demo` provides a small catalogue and logs the shortest chain length.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a begin code HIT, an end code COG, and a catalogue of six codes. Step 1: we load the catalogue into a hash set, confirm COG is present, and enqueue HIT at step one. Step 2: at level one we expand HIT, and the only valid one-letter neighbour is HOT, which we enqueue and remove from the set; steps becomes two. Step 3: at level two we expand HOT, finding DOT and LOT, enqueue both, and steps becomes three. Step 4: at level three we expand DOT and LOT, discovering DOG and LOG, and steps becomes four. Step 5: at level four we expand DOG and reach COG, enqueue it, and steps becomes five. Step 6: at level five we poll COG, it equals the end, and we return a chain length of five.

```

INFO: Shortest code chain length = 5

```

```
    │

  queue=[hot] step=2
    │

  queue=[dog,log] step=4
    │
    ▼  level 4: expand dog → cog
  queue=[cog] step=5
    │
    ▼  level 5: poll cog == end
  Output: chain length = 5  (hit→hot→dot→dog→cog)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Ladder is a shortest path problem hiding behind a string puzzle. I treat each word as a node in an implicit graph, with an edge between any two words that differ by exactly one letter, and because every such edge costs the same single step, breadth-first search from the begin word finds the fewest transformations to reach the end word. I never build the graph explicitly; instead I generate each word's neighbours on the fly by trying every single-letter substitution and keeping only the results that exist in the dictionary.

The two details that make this efficient are a hash set for the dictionary, which gives constant-time membership checks, and removing each word from that set the moment I enqueue it, which doubles as a visited marker so I never process the same word twice. I process the queue level by level, incrementing the step count after each level, so the first time I dequeue the end word its distance is exactly the shortest chain length. For large dictionaries I would reach for bidirectional BFS, searching from both ends and meeting in the middle, which shrinks the explored frontier dramatically.

At the National Bank of India I used this shape for a product-code migration where compliance required every intermediate code to be a valid catalogue code and only one character could change per step. I loaded the catalogue into a set cached in Redis and ran the level-by-level search to find the shortest compliant chain from the old code to the new one. Explaining the implicit graph, the on-the-fly neighbour generation, and the set-as-visited trick is what shows an interviewer I can recognise a shortest path problem even when it is dressed up as string manipulation.
